fields.apa_citation: Axelsson, Ö., Nilsson, M. E., & Berglund, B. (2010). A principal components model of soundscape perception. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 128(5), 2836-2846. https://doi.org/10.1121/1.3493436
fields.main_conclusion: Soundscape perception is well described by three basic perceptual components (Pleasantness, Eventfulness, Familiarity), and the dominant category of sound in a soundscape (technological, natural, or human) predicts its position on the Pleasantness and Eventfulness dimensions even after controlling for overall loudness.
independent_variables: Dominant sound category of soundscape excerpt (technological, natural, human, none)
Acoustic properties of soundscape excerpts (L Aeq,30s, level variability, low-frequency proportion)
fields.construct_pair: Dominant sound category (technological/natural/human) -> Pleasantness and Eventfulness of soundscape perception
fields.effect_size: R2 = 0.59 (Pleasantness model with N10 + sound categories); R2 = 0.55 (Eventfulness model with N10 + sound categories)
fields.stimulus_description: Listeners heard 50 30-second binaural recordings of urban outdoor soundscapes (from London and Stockholm) covering technological, natural, and human sound sources, played back over calibrated headphones.
fields.methods_surface_summary: 100 listeners each rated 5 of 50 soundscape excerpts on 116 attribute scales (visual analog 'match' scales); mean attribute ratings per excerpt were subjected to principal components analysis, and the resulting component scores were correlated and regressed against acoustic measures and dominant-sound-category codings.
measurement_inventory: A-weighted equivalent sound pressure level L Aeq,30s
L A10-L A90 and N10-N90 level-variability indices
L Ceq,30s - L Aeq,30s (low-frequency proportion index)

notes.independent_variables: Dominant sound category is the paper's main manipulated/coded predictor; acoustic variables are measured (not manipulated) predictors used as covariates.
notes.direction: Marked 'mixed' because the relationship differs by sound category: technological sounds -> negative (unpleasant), natural sounds -> positive (pleasant, though weak/less clear), human sounds -> positive relation with eventfulness but only weak with pleasantness. No single uniform direction applies across the IV's levels.
notes.p_value: The paper reports many p-values across correlations and regressions; the one chosen (p<0.01) is used for the split-half PCA reliability check and several key correlations (Table II); no single overall 'main finding' p-value is designated by the authors.
notes.effect_size: R2 values are for the two-step stepwise regressions predicting Pleasantness and Eventfulness from loudness (N10) plus dominant-sound-category variables (Tables III-IV), which the paper treats as its key quantitative result tying sound category to perception.
